A few days ago, OpenAI accused Apple of improperly adding new evidence in its trade secrets case. Today, Apple struck back, similarly alleging that OpenAI's response exceeded the scope permitted by court rules. Here are the details.

Apple says OpenAI crossed the line: it's not just about objecting to new evidence

In Apple's lawsuit accusing two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products of misappropriating trade secrets, one of the disputed points involves the application for a temporary restraining order.

In short, Apple has requested the court to issue a temporary restraining order, arguing that this would prevent its trade secrets from being further incorporated into OpenAI's hardware development during the pendency of the case.

In the legal back-and-forth over that application, Apple submitted an opposition brief accompanied by five expert declarations. The defendants subsequently countered that Apple had improperly introduced new evidence and asked the court to strike portions of the materials.

In their filings objecting to Apple's alleged introduction of new evidence, OpenAI and the other defendants also simultaneously submitted multiple documents to rebut Apple's arguments.

Apple today filed a response to those objections, arguing that the defendants are not merely objecting to new evidence, but are using the opportunity to introduce new arguments and their own evidence:

Rule 7-3(d)(1) permits a party to object to new evidence in an opposition brief, but also cautions that the filings 'shall not include further argument on the motion.' The defendants did not abide by this limitation, and instead used their filings to re-litigate the merits of Apple's temporary restraining order motion. For example, the defendants question whether Dr. Runge has 'any basis to provide an analysis,' whether he adequately responds to 'contradictory evidence,' and whether he can prove that some of Apple's materials are not public. [⋯] These arguments are not objections to new evidence. [⋯] (The argument that 'some of plaintiff's positions lack evidentiary support or are undermined by other evidence' is 'not an objection to evidence.')

Apple also took issue with a new declaration submitted by Liu, describing it as 'the most egregious overreach' in the defendants' filings:

It is worth noting that, when submitting Liu's declaration, the defendants had argued that the court should only consider that document when deciding which of Apple's challenged evidence to take into account.

That said, Apple pointed out that since the defendants have now raised new arguments on their own, the court should consider the entire record rather than striking any evidence from Apple's opposition brief:

The court is scheduled to hear Apple's application for a temporary restraining order on October 14.
